articles.content: SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — Seoul said Friday that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South. South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it let the six others return to North Korea aboard their boat across the Koreas’ eastern maritime border Friday morning. The North Koreans were rescued by South Korea’s navy and coast guard in international waters near South Korea’s eastern Ulleung Island on Nov. 3. It’s not uncommon for North Korean fishing boats to be found adrift south of the Koreas’ eastern and western sea boundaries. South Korea typically returns North Korean fishermen if they want to go home and are not suspected of espionage. But South Korea lets them resettle in the South if they so choose. North Korea has yet to comment on the fisherman who opted to remain in South Korea. Pyongyang is highly sensitive about defections and often accuses Seoul of enticing its citizens to defect, something the South denies. The two Koreas remain split along one of the world’s most heavily fortified borders since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice. Citizens from the two countries are not allowed to exchange phone calls, letters and emails with each other. More than 34,000 North Koreans have fled to South Korea for economic and political reasons since the war’s end, mostly in the last three decades. Animosities between the Koreas have deepened in recent years, with North Korea terminating ties with South Korea and focusing on expanding its nuclear program.

‘No future here': Why Senegal’s young people risk their lives to reach Europe
articles.description: ‘No future here': Why Senegal’s young people risk their lives to reach Europe AP News Around 175 migrants unaccounted for after contact lost with boat from Senegal Reuters On Senegal's shores, hopes of a better life in Europe persist despite the risks of migration, in photos Journal-News.com
articles.content: KAYAR, Senegal (AP) — Baye Coura Diop barely survived his first attempt to reach Europe from Senegal in a wooden fishing boat. The overcrowded pirogue lost its way and he spent 15 days adrift, with only seawater to drink, he said. On his second and third attempts, he narrowly escaped arrest by Senegalese authorities. Yet he is determined to try again and has already paid the smuggler as he awaits their green light to leave. “Half of my friends are in Europe,” said Diop, 23, sitting on a beach surrounded by empty nets and pirogues abandoned by owners who have left for Spain. “Fishing does not work anymore. There is nothing to do here.” Despite millions of dollars spent by Europe to reduce the number of departures from West Africa, Diop and many others believe that leaving is their only option to find work and build a better life. Legal routes to Europe are largely out of reach for ordinary West Africans, who face some of the world’s highest visa rejection rates, strict documentation requirements and invasive checks. Thousands attempt the Atlantic crossing each year in rickety fishing boats, taking a route so dangerous it has been dubbed “Barcelona or die.” More than 29,000 people, mostly from Senegal and the Gambia, have reached Spain’s Canary Islands this year, according to Spanish authorities. A record 16,000 arrived in November alone — three times the number recorded in the first half of the year. The spike in arrivals has become political fodder on the campaign trail ahead of Spain’s general election on Sunday. Conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo and far-right Vox candidate Santiago Abascal have regularly pointed to the migrant boats as proof of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s failed immigration policies. The arrivals mark a sharp increase from last year, when 17,000 people reached the islands as Senegalese authorities intensified European-funded surveillance, reducing departures. Earlier this week, the Senegalese navy said they intercepted five pirogues carrying a total of 974 people in a single day. But surveillance is not enough to deter desperate young people, fishermen said. Several pirogues have left Kayar under cover of darkness in recent weeks, taking advantage of favorable conditions before winter brings rougher seas. Around 75% of Senegalese are under 35, and most are either unemployed or working in the informal sector with no financial security. Senegal is grappling with a heavy public debt burden, soaring living costs and widespread poverty. Medical care is expensive and paid for out of pocket. Diop’s fishing town, Kayar, is one of the main departure points for Europe. Fishing is central to Senegal’s economy, accounting for 3% of GDP and supporting around 50,000 direct and 500,000 indirect jobs, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. But the fishing industry is being hit by climate change and competition from foreign industrial trawlers, mostly from China, Russia and Turkey, operating in Senegalese waters. European companies have also contributed to overfishing through demand for fishmeal and fish oil, as well as regulatory loopholes — environmental groups documented the practice of registering vessels under third-country flags to bypass regulations. “It’s the industrial boats — the government allowed them to fish, but they don’t respect the limits and come where the small pirogues are supposed to fish,” said Ngagne Cisse, secretary-general of the association of returned migrants. “It has been going on for a long time, and now we are seeing the consequences.” Ngagne Cisse poses for a photo in Kayar, Bayakh region, Senegal, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Carmen Yasmine Abd Ali) Ngagne Cisse poses for a photo in Kayar, Bayakh region, Senegal, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Carmen Yasmine Abd Ali) Cisse, 42, said fishermen earned a decent living when he was young. He was among the first to reach Spain on a pirogue in 2006, but was deported back to Senegal. Conditions for fishermen have worsened since then. “There is no more fish left for us,” he said. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was elected in 2024 on a pledge to improve the living standards of ordinary Senegalese, including by reviewing fishing permits for foreign companies. But fishermen say nothing has changed. “The new authorities said they would put an end to this. That is what we were expecting, but since then, we have seen nothing,” Cisse said. “If you emigrate, it’s because you’ve run out of options.” The number of people who have died trying to reach Europe across the Atlantic remains unknown. Between 2022 and 2025, deaths and disappearances increased by 95 per cent on this route. The International Organization for Migration has recorded more than 6,500 deaths since 2020, but that figure is widely believed to be only a fraction of the actual toll. Many shipwrecks go undocumented, leaving no trace of those aboard. Caminando Fronteras, a Spanish migrant rights organization, documented over 26,000 people who have gone missing or died since 2020. Among the missing is the husband of Falla Dionne, 24. He left home in July 2022, telling her he was going to Mauritania for work. Their son was just three months old. A week later, his parents told her he had boarded a pirogue bound for Spain. She has not heard from him since. “In the beginning it was very difficult, I missed him a lot,” a tearful Dionne said. “But recently I have started to pull through.” She said she does not blame her husband for leaving, even though it broke her heart. Despite his disappearance, she is preparing to make the same dangerous journey. She has saved enough to pay a smuggler and is waiting for the right moment to leave. She plans to leave her son with his grandmother, who has been his main caregiver since Dionne’s husband disappeared and she began working in a hair salon. Young people gather outside a house in Kayar, Bayakh region, Senegal, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Carmen Yasmine Abd Ali) Young people gather outside a house in Kayar, Bayakh region, Senegal, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Carmen Yasmine Abd Ali) While the Atlantic route to Europe can be deadly, the potential financial rewards remain a powerful draw. Families with relatives in Spain can afford to renovate their homes or build new ones, and pay for medical care when someone falls seriously ill. Diop, a 23-year-old fisherman, lives in his mother’s house with 20 family members. He and his older brother have each tried to migrate three times over the years, paying about 400,000 CFA francs ($669) for each attempt. “My future does not lie in Senegal, because the work is hard. You work a lot to earn very little,” he said. “When you want to help your family, you have to work a great deal to earn a significant amount.” He added: “Honestly, it’s not easy to even think about marriage because it requires money. So, as for my future? Well, I’m already looking ahead to Spain.” Diop’s mother, Sally Ndiaye, said she dreads waking each morning, afraid that one of her sons may have left. Yet she financed their previous attempts with community loans. From her window, she can see a new house being built next door, paid for by her brother-in-law, who made it to Spain. “Life here is just so difficult,” she said. “I no longer try to stop him from leaving. I pray to God to guide him in peace … so that we might help one another. It is poverty that drives this: out of compassion for their parents, they want to help them — and that is why young people risk their lives.” Associated Press writer Suman Naishadham in Madrid, Spain, contributed to this report. Michigan State basketball explodes in second half to beat Arkansas
articles.content: The Michigan State Spartans found themselves trailing by four points at halftime against the Arkansas Razorbacks, but they used a strong second half surge to power past the Razorbacks , 70-67. Following the win, Michigan State head coach Tom Izzo spoke about coming out better after halftime as the team pulled ahead and secured the victory, as per Chris Solari of Detroit Free Press. “The first half of basketball was ugly,” Izzo said. “I really thought it was atrocious. We gotta play better. All in all, it’s Thanksgiving. I’m thankful we won.” Michigan State exploded in the second half, dropped 43 points while holding Arkansas to 36 points. The Spartans held the Razorbacks to 40 percent shooting overall and 13 percent shooting from the 3-point line. In comparison, they shot 54 percent from the field and a scorching 67 percent from the 3-point line. The Spartans were led by projected NBA first round draft pick Jeremy Fears Jr. who finished with a team-high 20 points, two rebounds, 10 assists, one steal and one blocked shot in 32 minutes of play. He shot 6-of-7 from the field, a perfect 2-of-2 from the 3-point line and 6-of-10 from the free-throw line. Jordan Scott added 15 points and eight rebounds. Michigan State is in the program’s 32nd season with Tom Izzo at the helm as head coach. During that time, he’s led the Spartans to 28 NCAA Tournament appearances, including winning the national championship in 2000. The Spartans are coming off a season in which they finished 27-8, but lost in the Sweet 16 of the NCAA Tournament against UConn.

articles.title: Hundreds gather in Romeo for Thanksgiving Day community dinner
articles.content: Hundreds of people in northern Macomb County didn’t have to worry about cooking Thanksgiving dinner on Thursday afternoon. Instead, they opted for a free meal with desserts, some live entertainment, camaraderie, and a chance to see the Detroit Lions battle the Chicago Bears on a large-screen TV. The Lions ended up losing a thriller, but the crowd had a good time anyway. Among those at the Romeo Masonic Lodge on Main Street in downtown Romeo was Laura Spam, who said she might otherwise have spent the day alone if it weren’t for the event. She said a number of relatives have died and her sister is in the hospital, so she doesn’t prepare a holiday dinner. “That’s why I come here, as I’ve done for the past few years,” said Spam, a Rochester resident. “This is such a great thing and the people are so giving — they even send you home with food. And the best part is, it doesn’t cost you a thing.” Spam sat at a large table occupied by some familiar faces and made some new friends as well. She also brought along her “best friend” to the community event. “This is my first time,” said Karen Hall, the best friend. “This is so lovely. I would have been home alone. My son is at work — he’s a fireman for Detroit.” Those sentiments sum up why organizers plan the community dinner months in advance. James Routheaux, who works for Sheetz fuel centers, and Justin Parker, an electrician and elected Romeo trustee, have organized a free Thanksgiving Day dinner for the community for several years. The two are supported by a group of about 100 volunteers whose Thanksgiving goal is to provide folks a meal to let them know they are appreciated as well a little fellowship on the holiday. “This is all about fellowship and coming together as a community. We’re all here together,” Parker said. “To me, it’s all about everyone else. It’s about fellowship, coming together as a community. It’s about your friends, your neighbors, your family.” When the group hosted their first community event, they served about 50 dinners. Last year, more than 600 meals were served — including ones delivered for first responders in Romeo and neighboring communities as well as some businesses, like area gas stations. This year, they anticipated in excess of 700 meals will be served. Meals consisted of turkey, mashed potatoes and gravy, rolls, green beans, corn, stuffing, and more. At the dessert table, guests had their choice of several different kinds of pies, cupcakes and other assorted goodies. Organizers said the volunteers in the quaint northern Macomb County community readily sacrifice their own holiday to provide for others. In addition to Wendy’s, the event is supported by a number of businesses, including DEQ Property Services, Romeo Florist Flowers, Verellen Orchards and others. “We have to give back to the community,” Routheaux said. “Blessings come in so many ways and we feel we have to give back to the community.”

Henderson, Allen power No. 17 Miami to a 97-70 win over Michigan at Players Era 16 tournament
articles.content: LAS VEGAS (AP) — Shelton Henderson had 25 points, 10 rebounds and six assists as No. 17 Miami cruised past Michigan 97-70 in a consolation-round game of the Players Era 16 tournament on Thursday. Dante Allen scored 21 points for the Hurricanes (6-2), while Nick Dorn added 14, Aceden Lewis 12 and Malik Reneau 11. J.P. Estrella led Michigan (3-4) with 21 points. Trey McKenney added 16 points and Elliot Cadeau 15. Miami opened the second half with a 12-2 run to take a 64-47 lead with 15:29 remaining. Henderson scored six points during the outburst. Miami’s largest lead was 31 points, while Michigan got no closer than nine in the second half. The Hurricanes shot 56.3% (36 of 65) from the field, including 42.9% (9 of 21) from 3-point range. Miami’s largest lead of the first half was 52-43 with 53 seconds remaining. The advantage came during a seven-point run, sparked by 3-pointers from Reneau and Allen, along with a free throw by Allen. The Hurricanes took a 52-45 lead into halftime. Henderson had 17 first-half points for Miami. Estrella led Michigan with 17. Michigan held an eight-point lead, 21-13, with 12:32 remaining after a seven-point run capped by a 3-pointer from McKenney. Miami responded with a nine-point run to take a 22-21 lead with 10:26 left in the half. Miami: Will play the winner of No. 15 Alabama-Kansas State for fifth place on Friday. Michigan: Will play the loser of No. 15 Alabama-Kansas State for seventh place on Friday.

Lions fall to Bears in final seconds of Thanksgiving heartbreaker
articles.content: DETROIT (AP) — Caleb Williams took a shotgun snap, dropped back, looked left and threw a perfect pass to the back, right corner of the end zone where only Rome Odunze could catch it. Williams threw the go-ahead, 6-yard touchdown pass to Odunze with 3 seconds left to give the Chicago Bears their first lead of the game in a 39-35 win over the Detroit Lions on Thursday to break a first-place tie in the NFC North. “Rome is not even the primary on that one,” coach Ben Johnson said. “Caleb did a good job, just working through it, and the guys gave him a clean pocket.” The Bears (9-2) have won six straight overall and for the first time during the winning streak, they had to come back for the victory and display their resilience. “That mentality showed the whole world who we are and what we are,” Williams said. The quarterback, selected No. 1 overall when the NFL draft was in Detroit in 2024, had his midsection examined after the game. “Nothing showed up on the scans,” Williams said. Williams led the way, completing 30 of 44 passes for 345 yards with two touchdown passes after trailing by 11 points midway through the fourth quarter following Jahmyr Gibbs’ 70-yard run for his third score of the game. For the win and first place in the division, Williams lofted a pass to the right corner of the end zone and Odunze jumped to make the catch and got his feet in the end zone with a score that stood after a review. “It was a big game for us, and a big game for them,” Johnson said. “We knew it was going to be slugfest with a lot of fireworks.” The Lions (8-3) had won six straight, but couldn’t make a defensive stop to hold on for the win. “We did some good things, but we didn’t make one extra play,” coach Dan Campbell said. The loss spoiled another amazing performance by Gibbs. He had 205 yards rushing on 21 carries and three touchdowns — including a 70-yard sprint — and caught five passes for 47 yards, giving the dynamic running back 252 yards from scrimmage to match his total from a game earlier this month against New England. “Gibbs is special,” Campbell said. “He finds a crease and he goes. He’s electric.” Chicago became just the third team to rally from a deficit of 11 points or more in the fourth quarter to win on Thanksgiving, joining the 1980 Bears who did it against Detroit and the 1962 New York Titans who came back to beat the Denver Broncos on the holiday. The Bears had the ball earlier in the fourth with a chance to at least tie the game after Jared Goff’s pass went through Jameson Williams’ hands and was picked off by Dillon Thieneman at the Chicago 21 and returned 18 yards. Chicago turned it over on downs on the ensuing possession, going for it on fourth-and-3 from the Detroit 42. Gibbs ran for 34 more yards on the next snap that potentially set up a 50-yard field goal for a six-point lead, but Campbell went for it on fourth-and-4 from the Bears 33 and Gibbs was stopped short by T.J. Edwards with an open-field tackle. “That’s an incredible tackle that dude made on Gibbs in open space,” Goff said. “That’s really hard. We like our chances there and you tip your cap a little there. Gibbs was phenomenal and they made a great play there.” The Bears earned another opportunity to drive for a tie or the lead and faced a fourth-and-1 from their 41 and Williams converted with a designed run. Williams went on to make some passes to set up his game-winning throw to Odunze. “Heck of a throw,” Campbell said. “Heck of a catch.” Chicago’s D’Andre Swift, who was traded by Detroit to Philadelphia two days after Gibbs was drafted, ran for 65 yards and a touchdown and had 97 yards receiving. Goff was 25 of 36 for 313 yards with an 11-yard touchdown pass to Sam LaPorta late in the first half that put Detroit ahead 19-10. Detroit’s Amon-Ra St. Brown had seven receptions for 146 yards and Williams had six catches for 68 yards and a costly drop that took potential points off the board for his team and gave the Bears the ball back. Key takeaways from Lions’ 39-35 Thanksgiving loss to Bears Bears: TE Colston Loveland was carted off the field with a knee injury in the first quarter. DBs Kyler Gordon (shoulder) and Elijah Hicks (concussion) were inactive. Lions: Edge rusher DJ Wonnum (back) and safety Chuck Clark (hamstring) were inactive. articles.content: With the release of the prequel The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, franchise producer Nina Jacobson regrets splitting the Mockingjay films into two parts. At the time, The Twilight Saga and Harry Potter split their grand finale into two films, and Lionsgate followed suit, breaking up the last Suzanne Collins book of the OG Hunger Games trilogy into two films as well. “Even though I love the Mockingjay films, if I had it to do over again, I think both Francis [Lawrence, director] and I might try to do it all in one,” she said in an interview with Empire. She continued, “Mockingjay was such a big book, and it takes you to so many different places. But in the end, I think that Francis and I both felt that splitting them up… even if it did come from an inside-out place of really feeling like we needed two films to tell the story, I think audiences find it cynical. Even if its intentions are earnest, which they were. They feel like it’s a play to make them see two films instead of one.” Watch on Deadline With Collins’ two prequels like The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping, producers have changed the way they adapt the books. “We really put the burden on ourselves [now], even when it’s a big book, to transform it into a theatrical experience, to not take advantage of your audience’s patience, to make it as tight as we can,” Jacobson told the publication. “[Sunrise On The Reaping] is the longest by a minute or two of all of them.” The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping sees Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson return to their roles from the original trilogy. The film stars Joseph Zada playing a young Haymitch, and is joined by Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Glenn Close (Drusilla), Ralph Finneas (President Snow), Billy Porter (Magno), Maya Hawke (Wiress), Elle Fanning (Effie), Percy Daggs IV (Ampert), Whitney Peak (Lenore Dove), Lili Taylor (Mags), Kiran Culkin (Caesar Flickerman), Kelvin Harrison Jr (Beetee), Jesse Plemons (Plutarch), Ben Wang (Wyatt), among others. Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
articles.description: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.
articles.content: Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going. According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements. As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power. articles.title: Nvidia executives face scrutiny over alleged ties to China
Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
articles.description: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed exec with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair, is a Chinese spy.
articles.content: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week. What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question. Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8. The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.) Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang. None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency. The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets. The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind: There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
articles.description: Elon Musk's social network X has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see on the platform.
articles.content: After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter. The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen. The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging. The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn. X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform. “Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post. As required by the state law on large-scale renewable energy projects, developer Ranger Power will hold public […]
articles.content: Wexford Township resident Jake Kerby looks out at farmland. Early plans from a renewable energy developer could line the field with solar arrays. (Photo: Vivian La/IPR News)This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Communities will get a chance to voice their opinions about a proposed solar farm in northern Michigan next week. As required by the state law on large-scale renewable energy projects, developer Ranger Power will hold public meetings to hear from residents about the plan for Shipyard Solar, a proposed 1,600-acre project straddling Wexford and Grand Traverse counties. “It’s important that people show up. I think we all believe in our hearts that we have the best interest of the community and the public, no matter which side of the fence you’re on,” said Joe Porterfield, Wexford County administrator. Shipyard Solar’s total footprint, according to the developer’s site plan, would also include a battery storage facility, fencing and substations — adding up to just over 2,200 acres. Since the project was first proposed in the spring, there’s been fierce opposition from residents and some elected officials at local township meetings. Some say they’re not against solar power, but disagree with putting it on productive farmland. Dave Williams, Wexford Township supervisor, is against the project and expects a large crowd at the public meetings, more than who can fit into the township hall. “I feel if they don’t come and voice their opinion, they’re going to have to live with it,” he said. “If they want to change this and not get it through, they should be there and speak up against it.” Williams and some residents also worry about not having a say in what infrastructure gets built in their communities. “It would be nice if the local people could decide this,” he said. A controversial 2023 law limits the ability of local governments to flat-out reject big solar, wind and battery projects by giving developers an option to ask the state’s public service commission for approval. Democratic lawmakers passed this law and others in an attempt to help the state address climate change and reach its 100% clean energy goals by 2040. Critics say the law bypasses local control. An attempt to challenge parts of it hit a legal dead-end last week after the Michigan Supreme Court largely upheld the law. Since 2023, only one project downstate has been approved under the state pathway. Twelve projects are under review. Ranger Power is taking the state permitting pathway, after the local planning commission rejected a zoning amendment this summer that would’ve allowed the company to submit a local application. The developer hasn’t submitted an application to the Michigan Public Service Commission yet, but public outreach is one of the requirements. As this process continues to play out, it’s a balance between different priorities for some local officials. “I believe farmland is very precious. But I also know that there is only so much oil in the ground,” Porterfield with Wexford County said. “So at some point we’re going to have to figure out how to do things differently.” The meetings will be held at both the Wexford Township Hall and the Grant Township Hall on Nov. 30 and Dec. 1 at 7 p.m. Shipyard Solar public meeting info: Grant Township Hall November 30, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. December 1, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. Wexford Township Hall November 30, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. December 1, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. Learn more: How has Public Act 233 has shifted local control in northern Michigan?

articles.content: Parade goers try to stay warm as they line along Woodward Avenue in Detroit during the 100th America's Thanksgiving Parade on Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026.(Zena Issa)Tents and blankets lined the sidewalks of Woodward Avenue in Detroit on Thursday as families waited for the 100th America's Thanksgiving Parade to pass by. Prominent Michigan businesses, including Ford Motor Company and presenting sponsor Gardner White, marched along the route, waving to community members and handing out beaded necklaces and high-fives to excited viewers.Longtime parade-goers, like Victor Walker, recalled waking up extra early as a child on Thanksgiving Day to claim a spot with his family along the street. Now, with his daughter sitting on his shoulders for the best view, Walker said attending the parade is a tradition he plans to carry on with his own family."Now that I have a daughter and my son and my beautiful wife over here ... we just want to continue the tradition," Walker said. Taking it to these generations, it's a legacy for me."Other attendees remembered the parade looking a bit different in years past.Seana Smith said this was her second time attending in-person, but she recalled seeing broadcasts of other years."I think there were more, like, inflatable floats," Smith said.Nonetheless, surrounded by family and cheering for floats like one for Central Michigan University, Smith said braving the cold weather was worth it.

articles.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Devouring $85M Over Thanksgiving Weekend as ‘Focker-in-Law,’ ‘Hexed’ Launch
articles.description: Lionsgate's sixth film in its dystopian franchise looks to win its sophomore frame after notching series records with its debut Monday and Tuesday.
articles.content: Lionsgate's sixth film in its dystopian franchise looks to win its sophomore frame after notching series records with its debut Monday and Tuesday. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is claiming the head of the table at the Thanksgiving weekend box office as Focker-in-Law and Hexed enter the arena. Lionsgate’s sixth film in the dystopian Hunger Games franchise screens in 4,018 North American theaters for its sophomore frame, as it grossed around $15.1 million on Wednesday. Director Francis Lawrence’s adaptation of author Suzanne Collins’ 2025 prequel novel is looking at a five-day sum around $85 million to take its domestic cume to roughly $233 million through Sunday. The movie stars Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the first four Jennifer Lawrence-led films. Related Stories Movies Scott Caan Thought He Got a Prank Text. It Was Actually David Fincher Wanting Him in 'Cliff Booth' Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Eyes $270M Opening as 'Dune: Part Three' Also Heads for Big Start After opening to the fifth-biggest launch in Lionsgate history last weekend with $119 million domestically and $225 million worldwide, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has continued its momentum. The $150 million-budgeted film, which earned an A- CinemaScore, grossed $15.98 million domestically on Tuesday to notch the franchise’s biggest first Tuesday, narrowly topping the $15.96 million for 2013’s Catching Fire. Sunrise’s Monday sum of $12.8 million also bested the series’ previous top opening Monday of $12.3 million for Catching Fire. The East Coast has been impacted by a major storm stretching from the Midwest to the Eastern seaboard, leading the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to be moved to Saturday for the first postponement in its 100-year history. The inclement weather could slow down moviegoing throughout the weekend, including on Black Friday, which tends to be the biggest day for the box office over the Thanksgiving frame. Disney released Hexed in 3,725 North American theaters on Wednesday, with the animated fantasy film collecting an estimated $7.6 million on opening day, including $2.1 million in Tuesday previews. Directors Jason Hand and Fawn Veerasunthorn’s movie, which carries a budget north of $200 million, could be heading for a five-day launch around $35 million. This looks to be down a bit from the $45 million opening that the studio had initially been projecting. Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster lead the voice cast for Hexed, which centers on a mother and her teenage daughter grappling with the girl’s magical powers. The studio has been hopeful that it will continue to run throughout the holiday corridor and follow the lead of this year’s original animated features with pleasing performances, including Goat and Hoppers, although other recent originals like Forgotten Island have struggled. Earning an A- CinemaScore, Hexed holds a 66 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes. The Hollywood Reporter critic Angie Han wrote in her review that it offers “more than enough to make for a pleasurably transportive trip to the theater.” Universal Pictures’ Meet the Parents sequel Focker-in-Law launched in 3,382 North American theaters on Wednesday, grossing $5.3 million on its opening day. Director John Hamburg’s film appears to be in line for a $36.3 million opening over the five-day frame, also a bit below the initial projection in the $45 million range. Ariana Grande joins franchise returnees Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, as she plays a woman set to marry the son of Stiller’s Greg Focker. Meet the Parents opened to $28.6 million domestically in 2000 (en route to its $166.2 million domestic cume). Sequel Meet the Fockers launched even bigger with $70.5 million over the five-day Christmas frame in 2004, while 2010’s Little Fockers dropped to $45 million for its five-day opening frame. Focker-in-Law earned a B+ CinemaScore from audiences and holds a rough 29 percent critical score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for THR, critic Frank Scheck wrote that the sequel “feels like the nadir in a series that recycles the same tired jokes in increasingly desperate manner.” Disney animated features are known for debuting over Thanksgiving, as Moana 2 opened to a massive $225 million over the five-day weekend in 2024 to help that year’s holiday frame set the all-time record with $423 million across all titles. Last year, Zootopia 2 launched on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving and collected $158 million over the five days to help lead the frame to a combined sum of $290 million. The total for this year’s holiday frame is expected to rank below both of those. In limited release, Netflix launched director David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth on 252 Imax screens in North America. The Brad Pitt-led follow-up to 2019’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood appears headed for around $5 million domestically over the five days before it begins streaming Dec. 23. How did dwindling industry affect Detroit, Chicago and Milwaukee? | CuriosiD
articles.description: Deindustrialization hit major Midwestern cities, but not everyone recovered. The Curious Midwest series explores the differences. The post How did dwindling industry affect Detroit, Chicago and Milwaukee? | CuriosiD appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Deindustrialization hit major Midwestern cities, but not everyone recovered. The Curious Midwest series explores the differences. The Fisher Body plant in Detroit, pictured Aug. 9, 2017. Chris Gerben grew up in the metro Detroit area in the 1980s and ’90s. Even as a child, he noticed a lot of major shifts in the city. “We were a steel mill town and in the mid-80s is when a lot of this kind of emptying out of the city was happening,” Gerben says. He remembers going to at least three different elementary schools because teachers kept getting laid off. From the peak of Detroit’s auto industry until Gerben was born in the ’80s — roughly three decades — the city lost over 200,000 jobs. That’s more than during the Great Depression. It also lost over half a million people. Gerben now lives with his family in Chicago. He wonders if what happened in Detroit happened across the Midwest in the same way. How did deindustrialization hit Milwaukee? Why was Chicago seemingly spared? “If you don’t know any better…it would seem like, ‘oh, [Chicago] is privileged in some way,’” Gerben says. Deindustrialization shaped the Midwest in ways seen and unseen. For a limited series called “Curious Midwest”, WDET is partnering with WBEZ in Chicago and Bubbler Talk Milwaukee to answer listener questions about the connections between our cities. We look back at how things differed across these three cities when it came to the industries that built them up, and how each city dealt with the fallout. Over 100 years ago, the “Big Three” – GM, Ford and Chrysler – made a home in Detroit, which led to more cars being built in the Motor City than anywhere in the world. These factory jobs attracted the first wave of the Great Migration — African Americans leaving the rural South for the urban North, starting in the 1910s — as well as immigrant workers. Marsha Battle-Philpot said her dad, Joe Von Battle, was one of those early workers coming up from Georgia. “The auto industry here allowed for a relative prosperity that was unprecedented,” Battle-Philpot says. “It’s sort of not viewed like that with all the bells and whistles of say, a New York, but this place is no joke.” Von Battle was laid off from the auto plant when white workers returned to the factory after World War II. This gave rise to the axion, “last hired, first fired” with regards to Black workers. “He was so despondent about having to have faced a reversal like that, he vowed at that point he would never work for another man,” she says. With the prosperity of the auto industry, Von Battle decided to start his own business. In 1945, Joe’s Record Shop opened. It was an instant hit. In the first two years, he had a stock of over $100,000 worth of records. But in the ’50s, the Big Three started pulling out of the city, moving to the suburbs for cheaper land. This began before the “Rebellion of ’67,” five days of racial unrest in late July 1967 during which 43 people died, hundreds reported injuries and police arrested more than 7,000 people. “There’s a whole narrative that says, well, Detroit was basically doing okay until 1967 and all the whites left, and then Detroit fell into decline,” Battle-Philpot says. “That’s just so wrong-headed. There’s no statistics that bear that out.” During the rebellion, Joe’s Record Shop — a symbol of Black art and opportunity that defined the time — was looted. “When my father walked back into that store…and he saw the destruction, I say that my dad really died then,” Battle-Philpot says. “He tried to reopen after that, but he was just unable to gather it back altogether.” Today, the Big Three’s headquarters are still in metro Detroit, but jobs in the city never bounced back. The story of industry and its demise echoed in Milwaukee: the home of beer and brewing, heavy manufacturing and iron and steel. Industry here was more diverse than Detroit’s all-in plan on the auto industry. With a bustling port and growing rail system, Milwaukee was critical. “Blue-collar in Milwaukee meant middle class,” says Adam Carr, a public historian and artist. “That’s entwined with the history of socialism here: that the worker was not a chump in Milwaukee.” Carr points out the soil and native plants now growing at Three Bridges Park – an old brownfield turned into a sprawling park, filled with walking paths built over a freeway that cut through the city. It exemplifies the city’s indigenous roots, its peak in industry and the decline. The loss of jobs and wealth in Milwaukee, specifically Black and brown Milwaukee, went down just like in Detroit. Urban renewal and redlining stunted generational wealth — a history the city is still dealing with. Like Detroit, industry jobs never bounced back. “I heard someone say, pie in the sky in Milwaukee was the factory job,” Carr remembers. “We thought the gravy train would never end. I think we haven’t found exactly who we are after industry yet.” Both Milwaukee and Detroit are figuring out what comes next. But if there is a Midwest city that at least appears to have figured out its next chapter, it’s Chicago. In Chicago’s West Loop neighborhood, built on a graveyard of old industry, you’ll find the University of Illinois Chicago’s Cuppa Hall and the Great Cities Institute. Matt Wilson is an associate director here. He has studied the long shadow of deindustrialization in Chicago. He says historically, the city had a lot of the same advantages of Milwaukee and Detroit: natural resources, a bustling port. But what separated Chicago was the rail system. As the country pushed west, Chicago became a major hub. “Chicago still has that identity of the crossroads, a lot of goods flow through here,” says Wilson. “It’s really easy when you go on the river to see barge traffic, and when you go to any of the ports that are around the city, you see the large-scale movement of goods.” Industry varied in Chicago. The famous Union Stock Yards was considered the meatpacking center of the world. And if there is a reason why Chicago stayed on top, it’s because in the 1980s, the city pivoted. “Chicago needs to compete with other cities to attract jobs in corporate headquarters,” Wilson says. “It needs to bring in tourism, and, you know, make sure all the hotels are filled and that there’s a nightlife.” Tax incentives and tax dollars were funneled to rebuild downtown — but not other parts of the city. “The neighborhood of South Chicago, on the southeast side of the city, it feels like from the sort of historical archives I’ve read that the center of gravity was the steel plant,” says Wilson. In South Chicago, you had Pressed Steel, Republic Steel, Wisconsin Steel and of course, U.S. Steel. These plants were the source of middle-class employment, and stabilized the housing market and retail and commercial businesses. “Both my grandfathers worked [in the plants], my dad worked there and I worked there,” says Michael Lisecki, who grew up in the South Chicago neighborhood. “It was like everybody worked in one of the mills, whether it was U.S., Wisconsin, and I mean it was devastating when we all got laid off,” he says. Lisecki started working in the mills when he was 18, making better money than he ever dreamed possible. Three years later, he was laid off, and the neighborhood was never the same. Chicago pivoted earlier than other cities, which does separate it from Detroit and Milwaukee. However, no matter the city, deindustrialization left a hole. The work is happening to build something new, and it’s clear the bones of the past are still with us. Have a question about Southeast Michigan’s history or culture? Why Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's NYC event
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani called the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" ahead of Mohan Bhagwat's New York event. But can the mayor do anything to stop it? New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it. Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event." Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India." "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity. However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled. "Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity." The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims." United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more. India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities. The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
articles.description: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
articles.content: It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week. GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion). The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI. Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.” Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids. “We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch. That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI. “We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.” As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time. But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large. The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out. This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade. The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities. The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers. “The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.” Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.” Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI. “You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.” This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate. “Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.” GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms. The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games. The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect. Q&A: How Michigan could ‘make it easier to purchase a home’
articles.description: Michigan needs more housing. The state’s top housing official has ideas she says could help.
articles.content: Making homeownership in Michigan more attainable, and at an earlier age, must be priority in 2027, says the state’s top housing official That may involve tax breaks for seniors to help with downsizing housing, as well as preserving the state’s aging housing stock Also on the table: A downpayment assistance program to help first-time buyers get into homeownership quicker LANSING — Michigan created a new low-incoming housing tax credit and limited private investor ownership this year, but there’s still work to do to make it “easier for folks to buy a home in Michigan,” according to the state’s top housing official. “When you consider the limited amount of bills that got passed and signed this year, in general, I feel like housing had a win,” said Amy Hovey, who has served as the Michigan State Housing Development Authority’s executive director since 2023 – the first woman in the state to do so. Some efforts to encourage housing growth have stalled in the Legislature, however. The House has not yet taken up zoning reform bills backed by outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and bipartisan legislation to expand the Homestead Property Tax Credit has not advanced. Related: Michigan affordable housing advocates pitch $42M tax credit plan Michigan housing crunch sparks rare bipartisan push — and backlash Michigan houses are old and getting older. It’s a ‘huge problem’ for state Michigan is still facing a deficit of around 97,000 housing units, according to the state. But Hovey, who expects to stay in her role for another two years after signing a recent contract extension, will have allies in Lansing as she works to address the crisis. Democrats won control of all branches of state government, and many, including Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson, campaigned on housing affordability. In a recent interview with Bridge Michigan, Hovey said she wants to prioritize preserving the housing stock Michigan already has, making it easier – possibly through tax credits – for seniors to downsize their homes and streamline how money for housing makes it from various departments to those that need it most. Michigan needs to make it easier to buy a home “if we want to grow, if we want to retain and attract young folks,” Hovey said. “That would be a number one goal I would be looking at if I were (the Benson administration).” Read on to see the whole interview with Hovey. Questions and answers have been edited for clarity. Bridge: How would you describe this past year as it relates to the handful of housing bills that passed the Legislature?Donate Hovey: There weren’t a ton of bills that got passed, but the ones that did get passed are very impactful. … The state Low-Income Housing Tax Credit? Huge. I mean, the fact that will help us develop and preserve an additional 2,500 housing units every year — and it does not sunset? It’s predictable for developers year after year after year. While we know we might not always be in this (housing) crisis where we’re going to have to build, build, build, build, build, we are going to have to maintain all of the portfolios that we have throughout the state. … It helps sustain our development capacity — meaning developers from outside the state are now attracted to Michigan, who have not been here before. … I also love the baby steps in to (bringing) down the cost of developing housing, with the single-staircase bill(s) that got passed. Are there other things that we can do to bring down the cost of developing housing? Absolutely. But we kind of got our toe in there. Are there other areas that you could see the state making small regulatory changes, like with the single-staircase bill, that you think could spur additional developments? That’s a great question. I think making it easier for innovative housing types to be built across the state would be great. We need to update our building code to make it more predictable that modular housing components – or any type of factor housing, maybe in the broader sense – is able to be built throughout our state. I think it’ll allow us to attract manufacturers of factory housing to our state, because they’d have a more predictable pipeline there as well. I think a lot of our communities need some help with building that capacity of understanding those housing types, and the quality of those housing types. When you say factory or modular housing — some hear that and think of mobile homes. Is that what mobile homes are being rebranded as? It depends on who you ask, because people use these terms interchangeably. I love the term that people are coming to: Factory-built. That encompasses what we know as a modular home that has no chassis at all – it’s just built, moved, and then you’re never going to move it again – to a manufactured home, which … has a chassis and you can move it, then very easily move it again. Or, panelized homes, which are also very helpful in speeding up the development of housing. All of that’s done in a factory, so I like the broad term factory-built housing so that we’re not getting distracted by what we’re really talking about. Because what we’re talking about is getting high-quality homes developed in a fast pace. So, as you pointed out, the state Legislature was able to pass some things this year as it relates to housing — including capping the number of homes private equity can buy in Michigan — but did you see any areas of missed opportunity this term? We need to make it easier for folks to buy a home in our state. We see that the first time home buyers’ average age is creeping up. We’re now at 40. Forty. We want to make our state attractive to young people to move here, to stay here. We need to make it easier for them to plant roots … and we haven’t. I would love to see us take what we piloted in Detroit with the 40% downpayment assistance program and make that statewide. That would mean the State Housing Development Authority would pay 40% of a downpayment and homeowners would be on the hook for the remaining 60%? Correct — and it would be an investment, so it’s repayable. It’s not a grant, it’s a silent second, meaning they don’t repay on the mortgage until they sell … plus equal amounts of appreciation. So, if they use 40% of our funding, when they sell their home, they would repay our 40% plus if their house appreciated by 10%, we get 40% of that appreciation. It’s an investment in Michigan families, not a giveaway. … They’re still building equity, they’re still building wealth, this just helps them be able to even get into a home and to be able to build that wealth. But, more importantly, it gets them into a secure housing situation where the rent doesn’t keep increasing year after year after year. Are there other opportunities you see the Legislature being able to make homeownership more attainable next term? They could make it easier at helping our seniors be able to right-size their housing. Gov. Whitmer, in her budget, had a proposal for the current year that had mentioned a potential way to help seniors be able to get out of their big homes and move them into something more size-appropriate for them. That would help open up our homes for families, our larger homes for families. I think that’s an important thing to be thinking about. I do think it’s really important that we continue to help communities consider their zoning, make it easier to build in our built environments different types of housing that we know folks are looking for. You mention zoning: One large package currently stalled in the Legislature would reform zoning laws and allow more homes to be built on the same parcel of land. Do you think that will pass this year? I don’t know. There was talk that possibly there’ll be something yet this year, but probably not. Talk—meaning you’ve had conversations with lawmakers? I’ve just heard people say that maybe there’ll be something in Lame Duck but…no lawmakers have reached out to me going, ‘This is going to happen.’ This isn’t the first time this bill package has been introduced in the Michigan Legislature in some form. Is there a reason why we can’t seem to get it across the finish line if it’s good policy? I will say this: I think that everybody wants to see more housing in their communities, and I don’t see that a lot of local communities aren’t willing to look at their zoning. When the Legislature passed the Housing Readiness (Incentive Grant) Program, it provided us with funding to provide grants to local municipalities to change their zoning or update their land use policies to be more housing friendly. We went through that money very quickly for folks that signed up to want to do it. So, I think there is a will. Why the legislation is not getting over the finish line is a totally different political beast. But what I do feel comfortable saying is: I think everybody wants the same thing. It’s just how we get there isn’t the same. Local governments want to look at their zoning. They want people to develop housing—and that’s what this package is wanting to do. I think it’s just the folks not wanting to be told they have to do it is where the hiccup is. As we head into 2027 with a new governor, state House and state Senate — all of which will be led by Democrats — what would you say needs to happen for the next term to be successful in your eyes? We have been working on trying to get flexibility with our Housing Community Development Fund money. We’re going to work on that again next year. That will really allow us to be able to meet those local government and communities housing goals in a much better way than we currently are, with all the restrictions on that fund. Getting that legislation passed would be huge. We also are going to come up against our bond capacity. We can only lend up to $10 billion. We’re going to be pushing that this year. We need to get that increased. That seems like it’s administrative, but really important —because if we don’t get that increase, we would have to stop our programming. What would you want that bond cap to be raised to? What I would love is no cap, to be completely honest … or if we had to have a cap, it needs to be $20 billion. Because if not, we’re just back every other year and it’s a waste of everyone’s time and efforts. And when you say flexibility for the Housing Community Development Fund, what would that look like in practice? What we would like is for them to be able to say that we can use those funds for the development of housing … that we can use it for homelessness, that we can use it for capacity building — but that we don’t have to use it in any specific amounts to any of those different items. Right now, 30% (of the fund) has to go to homeless (assistance), 25% has to go to rental, and of that 25%, a portion – 20% of that has – to go to 60% and below, All of these things are needed. None of those activities are bad activities. They’re all great activities. But as the environment at the federal government … and the local government changes, we need to be able to move that number around as it makes sense. For example: If we were at risk of losing all of our homeless funding from the federal government … it would be great if maybe we didn’t have to put 25% to rental housing, because now we have the state tax credit that’s going to provide a lot of additional resources for rental housing, and we could put more of it … into homelessness.

John U. Bacon: Michigan's failed athletic director search shows 'utter incompetence'
articles.description: Sports commentator John U. Bacon on the Trev Alberts' money, Larkin's long-anticipated trade, and the legacy of Martha Firestone Ford.
articles.content: Nebraska athletic director Trev Alberts walks on the field before Georgia Southern plays against Nebraska in an NCAA college football game, Sept. 10, 2022, in Lincoln, Neb.(Rebecca S. Gratz / AP)The Detroit Lions are set to play a critical Thanksgiving Day game Thursday afternoon against a division rival. The University of Michigan’s search for a new athletic director has gotten far more complicated. And the Detroit Red Wings have finalized a deal five months in the making.For more on those stories and other sports news, Michigan Public sports commentator John U. Bacon joined Morning Edition host Doug Tribou.Doug Tribou: Nothing says Thanksgiving quite like contract negotiations and potential legal battles, but here we go. The University of Michigan was set to hire Texas A&M’s Trev Alberts as its next athletic director. Then U of M reportedly learned about a comment Alberts made during a legal deposition [about] when he was with the University of Nebraska. When asked about whether romantic relationships between a coach and a player were appropriate, he reportedly said, “It depends.” U of M rescinded its offer and there is likely to be a court fight over whether the university legally owes Alberts more than $17 million because of a memo of understanding. What’s your view of all of this?John U. Bacon: This is utter incompetence all the way around. And that might be generous. From Trev Alberts, from the search firm that failed to vet him properly, obviously. The [U of M] regents have not covered themselves in glory. And the new president, before she even starts — President [Cybele] Raver, that is — already has a big, national controversy on her hands. It's so weird, Doug. The last five years of Michigan athletics have never been greater — you've won a national title in men's basketball and football, and the hockey team's No. 1 — and never been worse. Look at all this. And Sherrone Moore, etc. So this is the wildest five years, I believe, in the history of the Michigan athletic department.DT: All tied up in this is the future of Michigan head football coach Kyle Whittingham. Michigan and Ohio State will play the 122nd edition of “The Game” on Saturday in Columbus. Whittingham and Ohio State coach Ryan Day are both getting a lot of criticism. Day is having his worst season, but Ohio State is still 7-4. Whittingham has fallen short of expectations, but beat a very good UCLA team last weekend. Are either of these coaches in a must-win situation when they meet in “The Game” on Saturday?JUB: Not quite, but it's getting close. Ryan Day is on a very warm seat at Ohio State two years after winning a national title. It's pretty incredible. In Whittingham's case, it all depends on who the athletic director is. Trev Alberts was expected to fire Whittingham regardless of the Ohio State game, so one never knows. I'm calling this the "Buyout Bowl" because I guarantee you someone's getting a large check for nothing.DT: [Laughs] Alright John, prediction time. Who wins, Michigan or Ohio State?JUB: Well, it's the Buyout Bowl! Michigan has an almost insurmountable advantage at this point [Laughs]. So that's that's hard to beat. The football game? Call it a toss-up. Who knows?DT: Michigan State will close out its season on the road against Rutgers Saturday. The Spartans got blown out by Oregon last weekend. If they win Saturday, they’ll be 4-8 on the season under head coach Pat Fitzgerald. Previous head coach Jonathan Smith was 4-8 in his second season and got fired. Win or lose this weekend, how much pressure will Fitzgerald be under next year?JUB: Almost none, believe it or not, because his team is getting better and better. They beat Michigan, don't forget. Michigan is the only team to lose to Michigan State in the Big Ten this year. The irony here, Doug? Of the three coaches we've mentioned, Pat Fitzgerald is in the safest seat at 4-8. Go figure.DT: Let's turn to the NFL. The Lions play on Thanksgiving Day every year. And you don’t get many better showdowns — on paper at least — than the 2026 edition. The Lions will host the Chicago Bears at Ford Field. The Bears have won five straight games. The Lions have won six straight. Both teams are 8-2 on the season. The winner will be in first place in the NFC North. What has impressed you most during this winning streak for Detroit, which followed sort of a shaky start to the season?JUB: That's true. A few things. One, the offense might be the best in the NFL and does not get the credit for it. Jared Goff, the quarterback, is underrated and having a great season. Jahmyr Gibbs, the running back, might be the best in the NFL. Amon-Ra St. Brown, the receiver, is also one of the best. What really impresses me though is that a pretty lame defense is doing quite well. And they'll have to do it again this weekend without their star, Aidan Hutchinson. That's what I'm watching for this week. Can that defense handle a first-rate offense from Chicago?DT: John, we also got news on Tuesday that Martha Firestone Ford, the longtime owner of the Lions, died at the age of 101. She passed the torch to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp, in terms of running the organization, several years ago. Do you have any memories or thoughts on the tenure of Martha Firestone Ford and her time with the organization?JUB: Sure. She was absolutely first-class. Never once threatened to move the team. Did not take the headlines. Did not do interviews. Kept a low profile unlike most NFL owners. Thinking of [Dallas Cowboys owner] Jerry Jones here, Doug. [Laughs.] And she did a great job leading the team. When she took over, things got better pretty quickly. And ditto, Sheila Ford Hamp.DT: Well, John, I don’t want to get into a rut, but this is when we typically talk about the fact that the Red Wings still have not traded their disgruntled former captain Dylan Larkin… but hang on, the script in front of me is indicating that Dylan Larkin has been traded, John.JUB: [Laughs] Wait, what? What? I'm not ready for this, Doug. I'm sorry.DT: [Laughs] The Red Wings sent Larkin to the Montreal Canadiens as part of a massive trade. The Wings are also sending two future draft picks to Montreal. In exchange, Detroit received center Kirby Dach, goalie Samuel Montembault, and current U of M junior and NHL prospect Michael Hage, plus four draft picks including first-round picks in 2027 and 2029. How did Detroit make out after months of trying to deal Larkin?JUB: I think very, very well. In fact, I'd even call it a win-win-win situation. All three parties — Larkin, the Canadiens, and the Red Wings — did quite well here. What they're really basically trading is their current star player, Dylan Larkin, for lottery tickets for future star players. That includes Michael Hage, currently at the University of Michigan. One little heartbreak there was his father. His entire dream for his son was to play for the Montreal Canadiens. He dies in a tragic accident, his dad does. And then his son is drafted by the Montreal Canadiens. So this does take that away. But on the grand scale, this is win-win-win. And it's better for everybody than Dylan Larkin on his couch in Detroit.DT: All right John, happy Thanksgiving. I'm always thankful we get to do this on the radio every week. I hope you have a great holiday.JUB: Well, thank you very much, Doug. Thanks to all the listeners who tell me on the book tour, every single stop, "I love Doug." [Laughs]DT: [Laughs]Editor's note: Some quotes in this article have been lightly edited for length and clarity. You can play the full audio of the interview near the top of this page.The University of Michigan holds Michigan Public's broadcast license.
