Where to live? From Green Houses to accessory dwellings, Michigan seniors have more options
articles.description: Many older adults face the dilemma of leaving their home and their community once it’s time to transition into a new stage of their lives. Communities have been working to implement many options to make this transition easier and to fit individual needs.
articles.content: LANSING — Many older adults face the dilemma of leaving their home and their community once it’s time to transition into a new stage of their lives. Michigan communities have been working to implement many options to make this transition easier and to fit individual needs. According to the AARP Home and Community Preferences Survey, 75% of older adults surveyed in 2024 wanted to stay in their homes and 73% wanted to remain in their communities as they age. But, 44% said they feel a move is inevitable because they don’t think their homes and communities will be able to support them as they get older. Those numbers have recently moved up to around 90% wanting to age in place, said Paula Cunningham, the state director of AARP Michigan. Paula Cunningham is the state director of AARP Michigan. (Courtesy of Davenport University) “I went through that with my own mom,” Cunningham said. “My dad died, and I wanted her to come live here. [But she said], ‘No, I’ve been here. This is my home. I go to church here. I know the neighbors here. I’ve got friends here. I don’t want to move.’” “You hear that often,” she said. “And one of the things is, sometimes people need to. It’s just time, not to get so attached to the physical space, but what’s best for you in terms of your health.” “When they have to move, what are the options?” “It depends on what you want,” she said. With an aging population in Michigan, communities through their local governments are planning to accommodate their wishes, according to Tom Hickson, the Michigan Township Association executive director. Hickson said 20% of state residents who are 60 or over live in Northern Michigan, including the Upper Peninsula. Donate Related: ‘Green Houses’ offer cozier alternative to Michigan nursing homes Michigan nursing homes have few staff, little training. Misery can follow Abuse, neglect common in Michigan nursing homes — and no one is coming to help Hickson said with any housing site, it is crucial to make sure there is proper infrastructure, available emergency response and adequate transportation that can appeal to multiple age groups. Every community has “different infrastructure, different needs, different populations,” he said. “One size does not fit all. Whether their needs be condos, nursing homes, or alternative housing, having this flexibility for making decisions at the local level on housing options is key.” That includes housing mixes for all ages and the ability of local zoning ordinances to best fit the needs of residents in their own communities, Hickson said. Tom Hickson is executive director of the Michigan Townships Association. (Courtesy of Michigan Townships Association) “I live a couple of blocks next to a facility that ranges from apartment-type living to living on your own with little assistance to intense care needs on their own grounds.” The Oaks at Belmont in Kent County is another example of an assisted living facility with options to meet the needs and wishes of independence of its residents, according to the Oaks’s website. Their options go from independent living on the top floor, like renting an apartment, to assisted living, memory care and rehab, and then more intense care services with 24-hour nursing on site. Hickson said not every community can support such a large operation. Another option is long-term care or living facilities, like nursing homes. “Nursing homes are highly regulated entities in the state,” Hickson said. “They provide a specific level of care, and when people need one, they really need it.” Cunningham said, “Sometimes you’ll have to go to a nursing home, and there’s nothing wrong with that. Just do your homework. Find the right one.” Another type of assisted living facility are Green Houses, facilities with no more than 12 residents and that allow for more independent living. Behind the name is the Green House Project, a nonprofit organization that creates non-institutional assisted care environments to support different levels of independence. According to the Green House Project website, the organization has helped to implement design and operational changes that give residents and employees at those assisted living facilities an alternative to traditional nursing homes. Green House homes came on the rise with increased funding for alternative options during the COVID-19 pandemic, Cunningham said. “The Green Houses that existed had maybe 1% or 2% of their residents getting COVID,” she said. “Compared to what happened to the nursing homes, some people were dying in nursing homes because there was a shortage of staff and the whole sanitary thing.” Cunningham said the AARP’s interest in Green Houses versus other types of long-term care facilities was elevated and there was money available then from the federal government to convert some facilities to Green House homes. Areas in Michigan that have seen Green House homes introduced include Detroit and Grand Rapids. Other communities have seen money going into these options because they are more cost effective, Hickson said. Cunningham said AARP also advocates for accessory dwelling units or “granny shacks.” Accessory dwelling units are extensions or additions on someone’s property, typically belonging to a relative, where older adults can live. “They’re becoming very, very popular,” Cunningham said. “Sometimes you don’t need a whole lot of space, but they want their privacy, but they still need to be connected to someone. “It’s almost like a single garage, and you just need a bedroom, a sink, kitchen, and they still have their independence, but the family’s right there,” she said. Earlier this year a House bill on land use, including zoning restrictions and growth management related to accessory dwelling units was introduced. The lead sponsor was Rep. Luke Meerman, R-Coopersville. The bill is stalled in the Committee on Government Operations. Hickson said, many townships allow accessory dwelling units and they are becoming more popular, given the economic situations of older people today, Hickson said. Regulations differ from community to community. Cunningham said dependency on family members or other caretakers isn’t always the right option because many older adults want to keep their independence. For example, AARP is looking into technologies called universal housing to make it possible for seniors to stay in their own homes. “They’ve got beds that lift you up. They’ve got robots that say, ‘Paula, it’s 3 p.m. Time to take your meds,’ and then the robot dispenses the meds,” she said. “Then I can pull my wheelchair over to get the meds out of the robot, sort of like a little candy machine out of the robot’s mouth.” Hickson said, “These people live in the same house for most of their lives, they get used to them. People know what they are familiar with. And change can become a challenge. [When or if] they can no longer take care of themselves, suitable options are out there for them.” This story was originally published in the Capital News Service.

Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
articles.description: Detailed estimate going back to 1800 shows how much carbon is being liberated.
articles.content: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it. A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note. Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Initiatives across Michigan aim to help older adults stay in their homes
articles.description: Throughout Michigan, groups are working to get seniors the funds needed to fix up their homes and make them more accessible so they can remain in their neighborhoods.
articles.content: LANSING – For older adults who want to remain in their homes as they age, an unexpected repair or a home that is difficult to navigate can become more than an inconvenience. It can become a reason they must leave. Throughout Michigan, groups are working to get seniors the funds needed to fix up their homes and make them more accessible so they can remain in their neighborhoods. For example, Capital Area Housing Partnership provides a service named Tuesday Toolmen, where retired volunteers construct wheelchair ramps for homeowners in Lansing and surrounding areas. “Most of the older adults we work with don’t want to move. They want to stay in the neighborhood where their family, church and doctors are, and they need help making that possible,” said Meaghan Redd, the interim executive director. Related: How to plan for aging in Michigan or take care of others: What to know Where to find help for Michigan seniors. A guide for navigating the maze Unlocking the secrets of Michigan’s ‘superagers,’ who defy golden years Redd said many homes in the region were built before accessibility was widely considered. Even a small obstacle, such as a step at the front door, can make it difficult for an older adult to remain in a home. “When needs change, older adults on fixed incomes often have limited options,” Redd said. “Accessible units can be hard to find, senior housing may come with a wait and rising rents add pressure.” The partnership’s Tuesday Toolmen program uses a group of retirees who construct wheelchair ramps. The organization also provides home repairs, rehabilitation and modifications that will make the home safe and help the homeowner stay there. Habitat for Humanity Northeast Michigan also aids homeowners with repairs through its Critical Home Repair program in Northeast Michigan. Roofs, furnaces, walk-in showers and wheelchair ramps are common types of projects for older adults, said Kristen LeSage, the program’s critical home repair coordinator.Donate “Ramps, bathroom modifications, widening doorways,” LeSage said, describing the types of changes that can help people age in place. LeSage said the program, which serves Alcona, Alpena, Montmorency, Oscoda and Presque Isle counties, has completed more than 125 projects this year for older and younger families. She estimated that about 70 older adults have been assisted this year. Affording repairs can be difficult for those living on fixed incomes. “Most are on a fixed income, and repair costs exceed what they can afford monthly,” LeSage said. Habitat for Humanity Northeast Michigan assists homeowners who meet the requirements established by each grant. These requirements may include having their name on the home’s deed, current homeowners insurance, up-to-date property taxes and household income at or below 80% of the area median income. Elsewhere, there is a new project being developed in Kent County which would work with older homeowners on their repair and accessibility needs. Chad Coffman, the community action program manager at the Kent County Community Action Department, said the Home Renewal for Seniors program is an experimental project aimed at helping eight to 10 homeowners 60 years and older by the end of 2027. Applicants must live in an owner-occupied, single-family home in one of 34 Kent County communities outside the city of Grand Rapids and have a household income at or below 80% of the area median income. This program would work off existing home rehabilitation projects in the county but increase the variety of repairs from whole-home inspections. “The demand for home repairs assistance has always far outpaced our ability to assist with the existing program,” Coffman said. The county’s current Home Rehabilitation program handles 10 to 20 projects per year with an average cost of around $25,000, Coffman said, but has generally focused on one or two major fixes, such as repairing a roof, furnace or electrical repairs. Home Renewal for Seniors aims to address multiple problems in a home. Funding will come from the federal HOME Investment Partnerships Program and the Area Agency on Aging of Western Michigan. Under the trial program, 25% of the cost will be covered by a grant, while the remaining 75% will be provided through a mortgage loan at 0% interest with no monthly payments. Homeowners will repay the loan when they sell the property or after 20 years. The program has already received enough applicants to meet its goal, but no projects have been completed so far, Coffman said. The county anticipates that it will begin its home inspections this month. Coffman said the issue of home repair cost has been recognized as a key factor in developing the county’s strategic plan for 2026-30. The county also expects its senior population to grow over the next decade. For Redd, helping older adults remain in their homes benefits more than the individual homeowner. “When older adults can stay in their homes, the whole neighborhood stays stronger,” she said. “They keep homes maintained, support local businesses and often care for grandchildren or volunteer in our community.” This story was originally published by the Capital News Service.

A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication
articles.description: Reed Berger-Fleishman, University of Illinois Chicago Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends. But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and […]
articles.content: Alcohol can magnify GLP-1 drug side effects. filadendron/E+ via Getty Images Reed Berger-Fleishman, University of Illinois Chicago Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends. But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts. For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different. As a physician specializing in obesity medicine, I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage. However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love. Respecting fullness cues Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes, obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb. GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer. Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol. In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging. One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changing fullness signals. Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate. These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving. GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors. A caution on alcohol Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking. Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience. Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment. Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions: Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication. Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal. Stay hydrated. Drink water throughout the occasion. Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms. The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms. Some injectable GLP-1 medications must be refrigerated. Storage requirements vary, so plan ahead if you’re traveling for the holidays. martin-dm/E+ via Getty Images Planning for travel Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment. Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. Storage requirements vary considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don’t assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time. If you’re flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Keep in mind that you might also need to have a note from your prescribing provider to carry them on. Arrange prescription refills in advance. If you anticipate needing a refill while traveling, contact your pharmacy and prescribing clinician ahead of time. Prescribing and dispensing regulations can complicate obtaining medications in another state, so don’t wait until you run out. Stick to your regular dosing schedule. Don’t take an extra dose or double up on medication to accommodate a holiday meal or try to suppress your appetite further. Taking more medication than prescribed can increase the risk of significant side effects and potentially cause an overdose. If travel disrupts your dosing schedule or you miss a dose, follow the instructions for your specific medication, or contact your prescribing clinician or pharmacist. When in doubt, plan ahead and ask for guidance rather than making medication adjustments on your own. Don’t sweat it with the occasional treat Perhaps the most important advice I give my patients is this: The holidays are not everyday life, and one large meal or dessert will not erase the progress you’ve made. You don’t need to skip Thanksgiving dinner, avoid your favorite dessert or feel guilty about enjoying a special meal. Maintaining a healthy relationship with food means allowing yourself flexibility while keeping your long-term goals in perspective. At the same time, don’t let one celebratory meal turn into several weeks of abandoning the habits that have helped you succeed. Enjoy the occasion, recognize when you’ve had enough, and return to your usual routine afterward. Reed Berger-Fleishman, Associate Clinical Professor of Medicine and Surgery, University of Illinois Chicago. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. articles.title: Why the Detroit Lions play on Thanksgiving Day every year
articles.description: The Lions' Thanksgiving Day tradition goes back more than 90 years. Here's a breakdown of how it started and some of the memorable moments along the way.
articles.content: 1934 photo of the Detroit Lions taking on the Chicago Bears in the first-ever Thanksgiving NFL game at University of Detroit Stadium.(Detroit Historical Society)The Detroit Lions will host their 87th Thanksgiving Day game when they bring in the NFC North rival Chicago Bears for a pivotal clash at Ford Field (1 p.m. Thursday, CBS).How did this tradition start? Here's a quick recap.How the Detroit Lions ended up with Thanksgiving gamesThe Detroit Lions have played on Thanksgiving nearly every year since 1934. The tradition began during the team's inaugural season in Detroit, after George A. Richards purchased the Portsmouth Spartans and moved the team to Detroit.Richards first became prominent in automobile sales before moving into the radio business. He purchased Detroit radio station WJR in 1928. At the time, the Detroit Tigers dominated the city's sports spotlight, so Richards drew on his radio background to help build exposure for the new football team. Part of that plan? Playing, and broadcasting, football on Thanksgiving.The first Lions Thanksgiving gameRichards reached out to George Halas, then the head coach and owner of the Chicago Bears, and the two agreed to have their teams face off in the first Lions Thanksgiving game. Richards saw an opportunity to boost ticket sales and generate national publicity for his new team.That first game - played November 29, 1934, at University of Detroit Stadium - sold out. An estimated 26,000 fans attended, while thousands more would-be spectators were turned away at the gate. Both teams were at the top of their division: The Bears entered with an 11-0 record, while the Lions were 10-1.The Bears won that first matchup, 19-16, led by stars of that era such as Bronko Nagurski and Red Grange. But both teams, and the NFL, benefited from the nationwide publicity generated by the game and its coast-to-coast radio broadcast. Detroit's annual Thanksgiving tradition was born.The Lions' Thanksgiving tradition over the yearsThe Lions enter the 2026 game with an all-time Thanksgiving record of 38-46-2.Since 1934, the only years the Lions didn't play on Thanksgiving were 1939-44, during World War II.The Dallas Cowboys began their own Thanksgiving tradition in 1966, when general manager Tex Schramm wanted to get his team more national publicity.In 2006, the NFL expanded its Thanksgiving schedule to include a third game in primetime, typically kicking off at 8:20 p.m. Eastern.From 1951 through 1963, the Lions hosted the Green Bay Packers every Thanksgiving. The 13-year run helped cement the rivalry as a holiday tradition, until the NFL changed its scheduling approach and introduced more opponent rotation.1962 - Thanksgiving Day Massacre: Detroit defeated the previously undefeated Green Bay Packers, 26-14, handing them their only loss of the season. The Lions' defense sacked quarterback Bart Starr 11 times in one of the most dominant defensive performances in Thanksgiving history.1998 - The Coin Toss Game: A late field goal by Pittsburgh's Norm Johnson tied the game and sent it into overtime. During the overtime coin toss, referee Phil Luckett ruled that Steelers running back Jerome Bettis had called "heads," even though Bettis maintained he called "tails." The coin landed on tails, giving Detroit possession. Jason Hanson subsequently kicked the game-winning field goal in a 19-16 Lions victory. The controversy prompted the NFL to change its coin-toss procedures.2004 – Peyton Manning's 6-touchdown day: Manning threw six touchdown passes on just 28 attempts as the Indianapolis Colts rolled past Detroit, 41-9. The performance came during Manning's record-setting season, when he finished with 49 touchdown passes, an NFL record at the time.2013 – Stafford takes down the Packers: Matthew Stafford threw for 330 yards and three touchdowns, while Detroit's defense sacked Packers quarterback Matt Flynn seven times, in a 40-10 win. The win snapped a 9-game Thanksgiving losing streak for Detroit.2024 – A Thanksgiving Day escape: Detroit edged past the Bears, 23-20, behind two touchdown catches by Sam LaPorta. Chicago had a chance to tie the game or win it late, but poor clock management left the Bears unable to get off another play before time expired.

This story also appeared in Chalkbeat Detroit The Detroit school district saw an increase in parent complaints about issues with their children’s schools and conflicts with staff in recent years. In response, the Detroit Public Schools Community District created a new office last year designed to handle those issues through restorative practices, which includes coaching through conflicts and checking in on parents’ well-being. The Family, Advocacy, Intervention, and Restoration, or FAIR, office uses parent coaches and DPSCD staff to help resolve issues in all of the district’s schools. Their work is also intended to boost enrollment and keep students in the district. The office handles issues ranging from facilitating restorative meetings between parents and school staff, as well as helping families navigate the student discipline process. The office was also formed to help parents properly escalate complaints through the central office, Superintendent Nikoali Vitti told Chalkbeat in an email. “School leaders also desired for more support to work with parents who are still learning effective ways to communicate their legitimate frustrations with schools and staff that avoid threats,” said Vitti. Tanisha Kuhn Sewart, a parent of five DPSCD students, said the office is helpful for parents who want help addressing ongoing issues. “If something needs to be cleaned up in the school, if it’s bad customer service … then that’s what that office is there for,” she said. Kuhn Sewart said she’s recommended other parents use the FAIR office, including one that was planning to leave the district due to frustrations with her child’s school. “She just felt like she was not being treated right,” said Kuhn Stewart. Two of the office’s goals are to strengthen student enrollment and retention, as well as “improve family favorability toward the district,” according to a presentation given by administrators in April. Increasing the number of students who return to DPSCD schools is a key strategy in boosting the district’s enrollment. While the district has improved in a number of areas in the 10 years since DPSCD was created — including chronic absenteeism rates, performance on state standardized tests, and filling teacher vacancies — student enrollment has remained largely flat. There were more than 49,620 students enrolled this fall, according to the district, compared to 49,717 in 2018-19. The fall-to-fall re-enrollment rate this year was 73%, according to DPSCD. The rate has improved by 3 percentage points compared to 2018-19. The district piloted FAIR at 31 schools last fall. It has since been expanded to all in the district. In 2025-26, the office resolved 96 issues with 20 parent coaches, according to DPSCD. More than 1,431 parents and guardians in the district received coaching and there were 58 targeted trainings and workshops for administrators and school staff. The office dealt with five restriction letter appeals last school year. Restriction letters, which limit access to schools, are issued in some cases when parents or guardians cause disruptions. There were 56 issued in 2025-26, according to DPSCD. The restrictions are lifted at the end of each school year. The office also mediated student incidents that involved multiple families, “so that students and families could safely participate in graduation activities,” said Vitti. Parent coaches get a monthly stipend of up to $400 a month. They are trained in de-escalating conflicts, advocacy, and navigating district and community resources. Sharlonda Buckman, DPSCD’s chief external engagement officer, said the coaching consists of dialogue with parents, helping navigate resources, and referring parents to administrators when necessary. Hannah Dellinger covers Detroit schools for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at hdellinger@chalkbeat.org. Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

articles.title: Thousands protest in Irbil as Baghdad moves to seize Kurdish oil and border control
articles.description: Thousands protest in Irbil as Baghdad moves to seize Kurdish oil and border control AP News Iraqi Kurds protest against Baghdad leader's moves to assert central control Reuters Trump backs Iraqi PM’s oil smuggling crackdown Al Jazeera Iraq’s Prime Minister Aims to Wrest More Power From Kurdistan Region The New York Times Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at plans for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings
articles.content: IRBIL, Iraq (AP) — Thousands of demonstrators gathered Thursday in Irbil, the capital of Iraq’s semiautonomous northern Kurdish region, protesting a move by the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced the measures Tuesday, describing them as steps to address oil smuggling. The decision marked a new escalation in a long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities and spurred rival Kurdish parties to come together in opposition to Baghdad. Al-Zaidi — who took office earlier this year with the backing of U.S. President Donald Trump — has been trying to assert authority on several fronts, including sending security forces into an area long controlled by a powerful Iran-backed militia last week. Tuesday’s decision brings official and unofficial border crossings in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces to it. Al-Zaidi also dismissed Kirkuk’s operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflect Iraq’s “independent national will.” Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court on Wednesday backed Baghdad’s move and ruled that federal authorities may deploy troops to secure all of Iraq’s international borders, “including the borders located within the territories administered by the Kurdistan Region.” Defense Ministry spokesman Maj. Gen. Yahya Rasool said Wednesday evening that al-Zaidi, who is also commander in chief, had ordered the deployment of military units to Kirkuk and other provinces and had ordered dirt roads used for oil smuggling to be blocked. Iraq’s Kurds have governed themselves since 1991, and the 2005 constitution recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But since 2003, Irbil and Baghdad have struggled for control over land, oil and money. The Kurdish regional government’s cabinet said Wednesday that al-Zaidi’s order “violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region” and represents “an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime.” It accused Baghdad of using “military rhetoric and threats” to carry out a “premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.” The Federal Supreme Court said the Kurdish regional government’s authority covers only the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the U.S.-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein. Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week’s orders. The Iraqi constitution’s Article 140 was meant to settle the fate of the disputed territories, a band of land from the Syrian to the Iranian border that is home to Kurds, Arabs, Yazidis, Assyrians, Turkmen and other communities. The article called for reversing Saddam-era policies that expelled Kurds from the area and moved Arabs in. It also called for a census and a referendum by the end of 2007 on whether the areas would join the Kurdistan Region. Neither was held. Peshmerga forces took control of oil-rich Kirkuk in 2014, when the Iraqi army collapsed in the face of an offensive by Islamic State militants. Iraqi forces pushed them out in October 2017, weeks after the Kurdish region held an independence referendum that Baghdad called unconstitutional. The disputes between Baghdad and Irbil have largely centered around oil exports and revenues. The country relies on oil revenues for about 90% of its budget. In 2014, Baghdad suspended federal budget transfers to the Kurdish region amid a dispute over oil exports. Disagreements over oil revenues and budget allocations have since repeatedly delayed salary payments for public employees in the region. In 2022, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court ruled the Kurdish region’s oil and gas law unconstitutional. The following year, oil exports through Turkey were suspended after an international arbitration ruling found Turkey had violated its pipeline agreement with Iraq by allowing independent Kurdish oil exports. Exports resumed in 2025 under an agreement placing sales under federal government oversight. The Kurdish region’s own politics are also in turmoil. On Nov. 5, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan quit the government led by the Kurdistan Democratic Party, calling it “failed” and threatening to form a parallel administration. No new cabinet has been formed since October 2024 regional elections, and the legality of the current government is being challenged at the Federal Supreme Court.

articles.content: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.” In October, Character.AI filed for bankruptcy following years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and hiring its CEO, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs. The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed. Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

ElevenLabs in Early Talks for Funding at $33 Billion Value
articles.content: ElevenLabs, the London-based developer of AI voice and audio models, has opened preliminary discussions about a new financing round that would value the company at $33 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. Management intends to formally kick off the fundraising in the first quarter of 2027, though some prospective backers are pressing for an earlier start. The target represents a 50% increase over the $22 billion valuation the company secured in September through an employee tender offer. ElevenLabs raised $500 million in a Series D round at an $11 billion valuation in February 2026, meaning the proposed price would triple that mark within roughly a year. Revenue has scaled quickly alongside the valuations. Annual recurring revenue, which annualizes sales from a shorter period, has climbed to $700 million from $600 million in September, the people said. ElevenLabs declined to comment. Note: ARR figures are annual recurring revenue as described by people familiar with the matter. At $33 billion, ElevenLabs would carry a steep premium to other European AI developers. Video AI company Synthesia reached a $4 billion valuation in January on about $140 million in ARR, while French model developer Mistral AI was valued at €21 billion (approximately $23.1 billion) in September after passing $400 million in ARR earlier in the year. Revenue multiples vary widely across the sector, but the gap underscores how aggressively investors have priced category leaders. Appetite for late-stage private AI assets has been strengthened by Anthropic's record $107.3 billion initial public offering, which delivered large returns to early venture investors and demonstrated public-market demand for high-growth AI infrastructure. Institutions are increasingly competing for allocations in leading startups ahead of potential listings. Founded in 2022 by CEO Mati Staniszewski and Piotr Dabkowski, ElevenLabs has built its position on realistic synthetic speech deployed in audiobooks, gaming and enterprise customer support. Its commercial lineup spans ElevenAgents for conversational workflows, ElevenCreative for multilingual content and dubbing in more than 90 languages, and ElevenAPI for low-latency developer integrations. The company has also introduced real-time detection software that distinguishes human speech from AI-generated audio in live streams. Staniszewski has previously said the company could begin preparing for its own IPO as early as 2028. The voice-cloning technology at the core of the business is also drawing regulatory scrutiny in major markets, including the European Union and the United States. For investors, the talks signal that private capital remains willing to pay up for AI companies with visible revenue growth, even as public markets have grown more selective about AI spending. A successful round at the target price would make ElevenLabs one of Europe's most valuable private AI firms and set a benchmark for other voice and audio startups seeking late-stage capital. articles.content: China’s Z.AI Co (智譜) has fallen behind schedule on its next flagship artificial intelligence (AI) model, while rival Moonshot AI Technology Co (月之暗面) expects the interval between major releases could double from six months to a year or longer if it loses access to overseas computing power, people familiar with the matter said. The previously unreported details show how efforts by US AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic PBC to prevent distillation, a technique in which developers train models using answers generated by more capable ones, have slowed Chinese AI development. Washington’s latest chip restrictions threaten further delays. The measures jeopardize a key advantage that has helped Chinese AI companies challenge their American rivals despite years of export controls: the ability to develop competitive models at substantially lower cost. A US Department of Commerce rule that took effect on Nov. 19 imposes licensing requirements aimed at restricting Chinese companies’ access to large amounts of computing power from advanced US chips in overseas data centers, targeting a means of accessing Nvidia Corp processors without importing them. Z.AI, also known as Zhipu AI, had planned to release its next flagship model, GLM-5.5, this month but has yet to do so, two people familiar with the matter said on condition of anonymity. The model, designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters - a measure of its size - has been held up partly by increasingly effective safeguards against distillation, one of the people said. Z.AI had hoped to complete training and release the model by year-end, but the new US computing restrictions could push its launch into the first quarter of next year or later, the person said. On Monday, the company released GLM-5.4, built on an existing model with 750 billion parameters. Z.AI says a new design enables it to match the performance of models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters. Anthropic said in September it had observed nearly 200 million exchanges with its Claude models linked to suspected distillation campaigns, attributing them to Chinese developers including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴), Moonshot and Z.AI. OpenAI has made similar accusations against individuals associated with Moonshot. Anthropic has described measures it uses to detect and block unauthorised distillation, while OpenAI has also reported efforts to disrupt such activity. Beijing-based Moonshot is particularly exposed to the new US rule because it rents computing power to train its models and prioritizes overseas providers, a person with knowledge of its operations said. The AI developer internally expects its usual six-month interval between major releases could stretch to 12 months or longer if its overseas computing access is cut off entirely, the person said, adding that computing capacity available in China could not make up the shortfall. Its next flagship model, Kimi K4, could be delayed until around the middle of next year, the person estimated. Moonshot released Kimi K2 in July last year, K2.5 in January and K3 in July. Moonshot has stepped up efforts to rent computing power in Europe, a separate person familiar with the matter said, confirming an earlier CNBC report. It plans to approach Chinese chipmakers about using their processors for training, the person added. Safeguards against distillation have also slowed Moonshot’s development, the person said. As obtaining training data from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models has become increasingly difficult, Moonshot has begun distilling from models developed by Google and Meta Platforms Inc, whose latest releases have made them attractive sources of training data, the person added. articles.content: Apple Inc. removed Chinese AI developer MiniMax Group Inc.’s chatbot app Talkie from its App Store worldwide on Thursday following allegations that its virtual characters sent sexualized messages to minors. ABC News and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism on Wednesday reported that Talkie’s AI-generated characters had sent sexually inappropriate and abusive messages to children. Although both the Apple App Store and Google Play Store restrict the app to users aged 18 and above, the report found that its age verification measures were lax.
